stem: The electron in the hydrogen atom is moving with a speed of \(2.3 \times 10^{6}\text{ m/s}\) in an orbit of radius \(0.53\text{ Å}\). Calculate the period of revolution of electron. (\(\pi = 3.142\))
solution:
The period of revolution is the time taken for one complete circular orbit, so

\(T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{\mathrm{v}}\)

Here \(r = 0.53\text{ \AA} = 0.53 \times 10^{-10}\text{ m}\), \(\mathrm{v} = 2.3 \times 10^{6}\text{ m/s}\) and \(\pi = 3.142\).

\(T = \dfrac{2 \times 3.142 \times 0.53 \times 10^{-10}}{2.3 \times 10^{6}}\)

\(= \dfrac{3.331 \times 10^{-10}}{2.3 \times 10^{6}}\)

\(\therefore T = 1.448 \times 10^{-16}\text{ s}\)

Check: the corresponding frequency of revolution is \(1/T = 6.91 \times 10^{15}\) revolutions per second, and multiplying it by the circumference \(3.331 \times 10^{-10}\text{ m}\) returns the given speed \(2.3 \times 10^{6}\text{ m/s}\).

stem: State any two postulates of Bohr's theory of hydrogen atom.
solution:
Two of the postulates of Bohr's theory of the hydrogen atom are the following.

**1. The electron revolves round the nucleus in a circular orbit.** The centripetal force needed for this circular motion is supplied by the electrostatic force of attraction between the positively charged nucleus and the negatively charged electron.

**2. Only those orbits are permitted for which the angular momentum of the electron is an integral multiple of \(h/2\pi\)**, \(h\) being Planck's constant. That is,

\(m_e \mathrm{v}_n r_n = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}, \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)

Such orbits are called stable orbits, and an electron revolving in one of them does not radiate energy, even though classical electromagnetic theory requires an accelerated charge to radiate continuously.

stem: In hydrogen atom, electron jumps from the \(3^{rd}\) orbit to the \(1^{st}\) orbit. The change in angular momentum is ________.
solution:
**(B)** \(2.11 \times 10^{- 34}\text{ Js}\)

By Bohr's second postulate the angular momentum of the electron in the \(n^{th}\) orbit is quantised:

\(L_n = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\)

For the third orbit \((n = 3)\) and the first orbit \((n = 1)\),

\(L_3 = \dfrac{3h}{2\pi}\) and \(L_1 = \dfrac{h}{2\pi}\)

The change in angular momentum in the jump is therefore

\(\Delta L = L_3 - L_1 = \dfrac{(3 - 1)h}{2\pi} = \dfrac{h}{\pi}\)

\(= \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{3.142}\)

\(\therefore \Delta L = 2.11 \times 10^{-34}\text{ Js}\)

Since the electron moves to the orbit of smaller \(n\), its angular momentum decreases by this amount.

Check: the change must itself be a whole-number multiple of \(h/2\pi = 1.055 \times 10^{-34}\text{ Js}\), and \(2.11 \times 10^{-34}\) divided by \(1.055 \times 10^{-34}\) is exactly 2, the difference of the two orbit numbers.

stem: Energy of an electron in the second Bohr orbit is \(- 3.4\text{ eV}\). Calculate the energy of an electron in the third Bohr orbit.
solution:
The energy of the electron in the \(n^{th}\) Bohr orbit of hydrogen is inversely proportional to \(n^{2}\):

\(E_n = -\dfrac{13.6}{n^{2}}\text{ eV}\)

Taking the ratio for the third and the second orbit,

\(\dfrac{E_3}{E_2} = \dfrac{2^{2}}{3^{2}} = \dfrac{4}{9}\)

\(\therefore E_3 = \dfrac{4}{9} \times E_2 = \dfrac{4}{9} \times (-3.4)\)

\(\therefore E_3 = -1.51\text{ eV}\)

Check: the given \(E_2 = -3.4\text{ eV}\) implies \(E_1 = 2^{2} \times (-3.4) = -13.6\text{ eV}\), the ground state energy of hydrogen, and \(-13.6/3^{2}\) is indeed \(-1.51\text{ eV}\). The energy is negative, as it must be for a bound electron, and smaller in magnitude than \(E_2\), as it must be for an orbit further from the nucleus.

stem: What is the mathematical formula for third postulate of Bohr's atomic model?
solution:
Following the order in which the three postulates of Bohr's atomic model are stated, the third postulate is the one governing transitions between orbits: an electron can make a transition from an orbit of higher energy \(E_m\) to an orbit of lower energy \(E_n\), and the difference of the two energies is emitted as a single photon.

Its mathematical form is

\(h\nu = E_m - E_n\)

where \(\nu\) is the frequency of the emitted photon and \(h\) is Planck's constant.

Since \(\nu = c/\lambda\), the same postulate written in terms of the wavelength \(\lambda\) of the emitted radiation is

\(\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = E_m - E_n\)

stem: Derive an expression for the radius of the \(n^{th}\) Bohr orbit of the electron in hydrogen atom.
solution:
Consider an electron of mass \(m_e\) and charge \(-e\) revolving with speed \(\mathrm{v}_n\) in a circular orbit of radius \(r_n\) about the nucleus of a hydrogen atom, whose charge is \(+e\).

**The centripetal force.** The electrostatic force of attraction between the nucleus and the electron supplies the centripetal force needed for the circular motion:

\(\dfrac{m_e \mathrm{v}_n^{2}}{r_n} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{e^{2}}{r_n^{2}}\)

\(\therefore m_e \mathrm{v}_n^{2} = \dfrac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r_n} \qquad \ldots (1)\)

**Bohr's quantisation condition.** By the second postulate, the angular momentum of the electron in a stable orbit is an integral multiple of \(h/2\pi\):

\(m_e \mathrm{v}_n r_n = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\)

\(\therefore \mathrm{v}_n = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi m_e r_n} \qquad \ldots (2)\)

**Eliminating the speed.** Substituting \(\mathrm{v}_n\) from (2) into (1),

\(m_e \left(\dfrac{nh}{2\pi m_e r_n}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r_n}\)

\(\dfrac{n^{2}h^{2}}{4\pi^{2} m_e r_n^{2}} = \dfrac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r_n}\)

Cancelling one factor of \(r_n\) and rearranging,

\(\therefore r_n = \dfrac{n^{2}h^{2}\varepsilon_0}{\pi m_e e^{2}}\)

This is the required expression. Every quantity in it except \(n\) is a constant, so \(r_n \propto n^{2}\) and the radii of the allowed orbits are in the ratio \(1 : 4 : 9 : \ldots\).

Putting \(n = 1\) and substituting \(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}\), \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ C}^{2}\text{N}^{-1}\text{m}^{-2}\), \(m_e = 9.1 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}\) and \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\) gives the radius of the smallest orbit, the Bohr radius,

\(r_1 = a_0 = 0.53 \times 10^{-10}\text{ m}\)

so that the result may also be written \(r_n = 0.53\,n^{2}\text{ \AA}\).

stem: An electron in an atom is revolving round the nucleus in a circular orbit of radius \(5.3 \times 10^{- 11}\text{ m}\) with a speed of \(3 \times 10^{6}\text{ m/s}\). Find the angular momentum of electron.
solution:
The angular momentum of a particle of mass \(m\) moving with speed \(\mathrm{v}\) in a circle of radius \(r\) about the centre of the circle is

\(L = m\mathrm{v}r\)

Here \(r = 5.3 \times 10^{-11}\text{ m}\), \(\mathrm{v} = 3 \times 10^{6}\text{ m/s}\) and the mass of an electron is \(m = 9.1 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}\).

\(L = 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 3 \times 10^{6} \times 5.3 \times 10^{-11}\)

\(= 2.73 \times 10^{-24} \times 5.3 \times 10^{-11}\)

\(\therefore L = 1.447 \times 10^{-34}\text{ kg m}^{2}\text{/s}\)

Check: for an electron bound inside an atom the angular momentum must be of the order of \(h/2\pi = 1.055 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}\), and the value obtained is \(1.37\) times this, so it is of the right order of magnitude.

stem: The radius of eighth orbit of electron in H-atom will be more than that of fourth orbit by a factor of ________.
solution:
**(B)** 4

The radius of the \(n^{th}\) Bohr orbit is proportional to the square of the orbit number:

\(r_n = a_0 n^{2}\), where \(a_0 = 0.53 \times 10^{-10}\text{ m}\)

Taking the ratio for the eighth and the fourth orbit,

\(\dfrac{r_8}{r_4} = \dfrac{a_0 \times 8^{2}}{a_0 \times 4^{2}} = \dfrac{64}{16}\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{r_8}{r_4} = 4\)

So the radius of the eighth orbit is greater than that of the fourth orbit by a factor of 4.

Check: \(r_4 = 16a_0 = 8.48 \times 10^{-10}\text{ m}\) and \(r_8 = 64a_0 = 33.92 \times 10^{-10}\text{ m}\), whose ratio is 4. The factor is the square of the ratio of the orbit numbers, not the ratio \(8/4 = 2\) itself.

stem: State postulates of Bohr's atomic model.
solution:
Bohr put forward three postulates for the hydrogen atom.

**1. The electron revolves round the nucleus in a circular orbit.** As in Rutherford's model, the centripetal force needed for this circular motion is provided by the electrostatic force of attraction between the positively charged nucleus and the negatively charged electron.

**2. The radius of the orbit of the electron can take only certain fixed values, such that the angular momentum of the electron in these orbits is an integral multiple of \(h/2\pi\)**, \(h\) being Planck's constant:

\(m_e \mathrm{v}_n r_n = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}, \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)

These are called the stable orbits, and an electron revolving in such an orbit does not emit radiation, even though classical physics demands that an accelerated charge should.

**3. An electron can make a transition from one of its orbits to another orbit of lower energy, and in doing so it emits a photon whose energy equals the difference between its energies in the two orbits:**

\(h\nu = E_m - E_n\)

where \(E_m\) and \(E_n\) are the energies of the electron in the outer and the inner orbit and \(\nu\) is the frequency of the emitted photon.

stem: What is binding energy of a hydrogen atom?
solution:
The binding energy of an electron in an atom is the energy with which the electron is bound to the nucleus, that is, the minimum energy that must be supplied to the electron in its orbit to take it completely away from the nucleus, to \(r \rightarrow \infty\), where its total energy is zero.

For hydrogen the electron in the ground state \((n = 1)\) has total energy

\(E_1 = -\dfrac{13.6}{1^{2}} = -13.6\text{ eV}\)

so the energy that must be supplied to raise its total energy from \(-13.6\text{ eV}\) to zero is

\(\therefore\) binding energy \(= 0 - (-13.6) = 13.6\text{ eV}\)

Equivalently, \(13.6\text{ eV}\) of energy is released when a proton and a free electron, initially far apart and at rest, come together to form a hydrogen atom in its ground state. Numerically the binding energy of the hydrogen atom is the same as its ionisation energy, \(13.6\text{ eV}\), which is \(2.18 \times 10^{-18}\text{ J}\).

stem: Calculate the change in angular momentum of electron when it jumps from third orbit to first orbit in hydrogen atom.
solution:
By Bohr's second postulate the angular momentum of the electron in the \(n^{th}\) orbit is an integral multiple of \(h/2\pi\):

\(L_n = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\)

For the third orbit \((n = 3)\) and the first orbit \((n = 1)\),

\(L_3 = \dfrac{3h}{2\pi}\) and \(L_1 = \dfrac{h}{2\pi}\)

The change in angular momentum when the electron jumps from the third orbit to the first orbit is therefore

\(\Delta L = L_3 - L_1 = \dfrac{(3 - 1)h}{2\pi} = \dfrac{h}{\pi}\)

\(= \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{3.142}\)

\(\therefore \Delta L = 2.109 \times 10^{-34}\text{ kg m}^{2}\text{/s}\)

Since the electron moves to the orbit of smaller \(n\), its angular momentum decreases by this amount.

Check: the change must be a whole-number multiple of \(h/2\pi = 1.055 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}\), and \(2.109 \times 10^{-34}\) divided by \(1.055 \times 10^{-34}\) is exactly 2, which is the difference of the two orbit numbers.

stem: An electron in hydrogen atom stays in its second orbit for \(10^{- 8}\text{ s}\). How many revolutions will it make around the nucleus in that time? [Given : \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{- 19}\text{ C},m = 9.1 \times 10^{- 31}\text{ kg} \rbrack\).
solution:
The number of revolutions made in a time \(t\) is the frequency of revolution multiplied by that time,

\(N = f \times t\), where \(f = \dfrac{\mathrm{v}_2}{2\pi r_2}\)

**Radius of the second orbit.** The radius of the \(n^{th}\) Bohr orbit is \(r_n = a_0 n^{2}\) with \(a_0 = 0.53 \times 10^{-10}\text{ m}\), so

\(r_2 = 0.53 \times 10^{-10} \times 2^{2} = 2.12 \times 10^{-10}\text{ m}\)

**Speed in the second orbit.** The electrostatic attraction of the nucleus supplies the centripetal force, so

\(\dfrac{m\mathrm{v}_2^{2}}{r_2} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{e^{2}}{r_2^{2}}\)

\(\therefore \mathrm{v}_2 = e\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 m r_2}}\)

\(= 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\sqrt{\dfrac{9 \times 10^{9}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 2.12 \times 10^{-10}}}\)

\(= 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 6.83 \times 10^{24} = 1.093 \times 10^{6}\text{ m/s}\)

**Frequency of revolution.**

\(f = \dfrac{1.093 \times 10^{6}}{2\pi \times 2.12 \times 10^{-10}} = \dfrac{1.093 \times 10^{6}}{1.332 \times 10^{-9}} = 8.20 \times 10^{14}\text{ s}^{-1}\)

**Number of revolutions.**

\(N = f \times t = 8.20 \times 10^{14} \times 10^{-8}\)

\(\therefore N = 8.20 \times 10^{6}\) revolutions

Check: one revolution takes \(1/f = 1.22 \times 10^{-15}\text{ s}\), and \(10^{-8} \div (1.22 \times 10^{-15})\) is \(8.2 \times 10^{6}\), the same count.

stem: Find the frequency of revolution of an electron in Bohr's \(2^{nd}\) orbit; if the radius and speed of electron in that orbit is \(2.14 \times 10^{- 10}\text{ m}\) and \(1.09 \times 10^{6}\text{ m/s}\) respectively. (\(\pi = 3.142\)).
solution:
The frequency of revolution is the number of complete orbits described per second,

\(f = \dfrac{\mathrm{v}}{2\pi r}\)

Here \(\mathrm{v} = 1.09 \times 10^{6}\text{ m/s}\), \(r = 2.14 \times 10^{-10}\text{ m}\) and \(\pi = 3.142\).

\(f = \dfrac{1.09 \times 10^{6}}{2 \times 3.142 \times 2.14 \times 10^{-10}}\)

\(= \dfrac{1.09 \times 10^{6}}{1.345 \times 10^{-9}}\)

\(\therefore f = 8.11 \times 10^{14}\text{ Hz}\)

Check: the period of one revolution is \(1/f = 1.233 \times 10^{-15}\text{ s}\); multiplying it by the given speed \(1.09 \times 10^{6}\text{ m/s}\) returns \(1.344 \times 10^{-9}\text{ m}\), which is the circumference \(2\pi r\) of the orbit.

stem: Draw a neat and labelled energy level diagram and explain Balmer series and Brackett series of spectral lines for hydrogen atom.
solution:
**The energy level diagram.** Draw a set of horizontal lines, one for each value of the orbit number \(n\), against a vertical axis marked as the total energy \(E\) of the electron in electronvolt.

- The lowest line, labelled \(n = 1\), is drawn at \(E_1 = -13.6\text{ eV}\). It is the ground state.
- Above it are the lines for \(n = 2, 3, 4, 5, \ldots\) drawn at \(E_n = -13.6/n^{2}\text{ eV}\), that is at \(-3.4\text{ eV}\), \(-1.51\text{ eV}\), \(-0.85\text{ eV}\) and \(-0.54\text{ eV}\). The lines crowd closer and closer together as \(n\) increases.
- The topmost line, labelled \(n = \infty\), is drawn at \(E = 0\). Above it the region is shaded and marked as the ionised atom, in which the electron is free.
- Each spectral line is shown as a downward vertical arrow drawn from the higher level to the lower level of the transition, because a photon is emitted when the electron falls.
- The group of arrows ending on the \(n = 2\) line is labelled **Balmer series**, and the group of arrows ending on the \(n = 4\) line is labelled **Brackett series**.

**Balmer series.** Every line of this series is emitted when the electron falls from an outer orbit \(m = 3, 4, 5, \ldots\) to the fixed inner orbit \(n = 2\). By Bohr's formula the wavelengths of its lines are given by

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R_H\left(\dfrac{1}{2^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{m^{2}}\right), \qquad m = 3, 4, 5, \ldots\)

with \(R_H = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\text{ m}^{-1}\). The first line of the series \((m = 3)\) lies at \(6563\text{ \AA}\) and the series limit, obtained by letting \(m \rightarrow \infty\), at

\(\lambda_{\min} = \dfrac{2^{2}}{R_H} = 3646\text{ \AA}\)

The whole series therefore lies in and just beyond the visible region, and the Balmer series is the only series of hydrogen whose lines can be seen by the eye.

**Brackett series.** Every line of this series is emitted when the electron falls from an outer orbit \(m = 5, 6, 7, \ldots\) to the fixed inner orbit \(n = 4\):

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R_H\left(\dfrac{1}{4^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{m^{2}}\right), \qquad m = 5, 6, 7, \ldots\)

Its series limit is at

\(\lambda_{\min} = \dfrac{4^{2}}{R_H} = 14586\text{ \AA}\)

so the whole of the Brackett series lies in the infrared region. The levels \(n = 4\) and above are close together, so the energy differences, and hence the photon energies, are far smaller than in the Balmer series and the wavelengths are much longer.

stem: Using an expression for energy of electron, obtain the Bohr's formula for hydrogen spectral lines.
solution:
The energy of the electron in the \(n^{th}\) orbit of a hydrogen-like atom of atomic number \(Z\) is

\(E_n = -\dfrac{m_e Z^{2} e^{4}}{8\varepsilon_0^{2}h^{2}n^{2}}\)

By Bohr's third postulate, when the electron makes a transition from an outer orbit \(m\) to an inner orbit \(n\) \((m > n)\), the excess energy is emitted as a single photon of frequency \(\nu\):

\(h\nu = E_m - E_n\)

\(= -\dfrac{m_e Z^{2} e^{4}}{8\varepsilon_0^{2}h^{2}m^{2}} + \dfrac{m_e Z^{2} e^{4}}{8\varepsilon_0^{2}h^{2}n^{2}}\)

\(= \dfrac{m_e Z^{2} e^{4}}{8\varepsilon_0^{2}h^{2}}\left(\dfrac{1}{n^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{m^{2}}\right)\)

\(\therefore \nu = \dfrac{m_e Z^{2} e^{4}}{8\varepsilon_0^{2}h^{3}}\left(\dfrac{1}{n^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{m^{2}}\right)\)

The wavelength of the emitted radiation is \(\lambda = c/\nu\), so dividing throughout by \(c\),

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = \dfrac{m_e Z^{2} e^{4}}{8c\,\varepsilon_0^{2}h^{3}}\left(\dfrac{1}{n^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{m^{2}}\right)\)

Every quantity multiplying the bracket is a constant. Writing

\(R_H = \dfrac{m_e e^{4}}{8c\,\varepsilon_0^{2}h^{3}}\)

which on substituting the values of the constants comes to \(1.097 \times 10^{7}\text{ m}^{-1}\) and is called Rydberg's constant, the wavelengths of the spectral lines of hydrogen \((Z = 1)\) are given by

\(\therefore \dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R_H\left(\dfrac{1}{n^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{m^{2}}\right), \qquad m > n\)

This is Bohr's formula for the hydrogen spectral lines. Each fixed value of the inner orbit number \(n\) gives one series of lines: \(n = 1\) the Lyman series, \(n = 2\) the Balmer series, \(n = 3\) the Paschen series, \(n = 4\) the Brackett series and \(n = 5\) the Pfund series, the successive members of each series being obtained by taking \(m = n + 1, n + 2, \ldots\)

stem: State the name of the visible series in hydrogen spectrum.
solution:
The visible series in the hydrogen spectrum is the **Balmer series**.

Its lines are emitted when the electron falls from an outer orbit \(m = 3, 4, 5, \ldots\) to the fixed inner orbit \(n = 2\), their wavelengths being given by

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R_H\left(\dfrac{1}{2^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{m^{2}}\right)\)

The first line of the series lies at \(6563\text{ \AA}\), in the red, and the series limit at \(3646\text{ \AA}\), so the lines of this series fall in and just beyond the visible region \(4000\text{ \AA}\) to \(7000\text{ \AA}\). Every other series of hydrogen lies either in the ultraviolet (Lyman) or in the infrared (Paschen, Brackett, Pfund).

stem: Determine the shortest wavelengths of Balmer and Paschen series. Given the limit for Lyman series is \(912\text{ Å}\).
solution:
The shortest wavelength of a series is its series limit, emitted when the electron falls to the fixed inner orbit \(n\) from an orbit with \(m \rightarrow \infty\). Putting \(1/m^{2} = 0\) in Bohr's formula,

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R_H\left(\dfrac{1}{n^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{m^{2}}\right) \quad \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{1}{\lambda_{\min}} = \dfrac{R_H}{n^{2}}\)

\(\therefore \lambda_{\min} = \dfrac{n^{2}}{R_H}\)

so the shortest wavelength of a series is proportional to \(n^{2}\).

The Lyman series has \(n = 1\), so the value given in the question fixes the constant:

\(\dfrac{1}{R_H} = 912\text{ \AA}\)

**Balmer series** \((n = 2)\):

\(\lambda_{\min} = \dfrac{2^{2}}{R_H} = 4 \times 912\)

\(\therefore \lambda_{\min} = 3648\text{ \AA}\)

**Paschen series** \((n = 3)\):

\(\lambda_{\min} = \dfrac{3^{2}}{R_H} = 9 \times 912\)

\(\therefore \lambda_{\min} = 8208\text{ \AA}\)

Check: \(1/R_H = 912\text{ \AA} = 9.12 \times 10^{-8}\text{ m}\) gives \(R_H = 1.096 \times 10^{7}\text{ m}^{-1}\), in agreement with the accepted value \(1.097 \times 10^{7}\text{ m}^{-1}\); and the three limits stand in the ratio \(1 : 4 : 9\), as \(\lambda_{\min} \propto n^{2}\) requires.

stem: Calculate the wavelength of the first two lines in Balmer series of hydrogen atom.
solution:
The wavelengths of the lines of the Balmer series, for which the fixed inner orbit number is \(n = 2\), are given by Bohr's formula

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R_H\left(\dfrac{1}{2^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{m^{2}}\right), \qquad m = 3, 4, 5, \ldots\)

with \(R_H = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\text{ m}^{-1}\). The first two lines of the series have \(m = 3\) and \(m = 4\).

**First line** \((m = 3)\):

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda_1} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{9}\right) = 1.097 \times 10^{7} \times \dfrac{5}{36}\)

\(= 1.524 \times 10^{6}\text{ m}^{-1}\)

\(\therefore \lambda_1 = 6.563 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m} = 6563\text{ \AA}\)

**Second line** \((m = 4)\):

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda_2} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{16}\right) = 1.097 \times 10^{7} \times \dfrac{3}{16}\)

\(= 2.057 \times 10^{6}\text{ m}^{-1}\)

\(\therefore \lambda_2 = 4.862 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m} = 4862\text{ \AA}\)

Check: the transition from \(m = 3\) releases less energy than that from \(m = 4\), so \(\lambda_1\) must be the longer of the two, and it is. Both wavelengths are longer than the series limit \(2^{2}/R_H = 3646\text{ \AA}\), as every line of the series must be, and both lie in the visible region, the first in the red and the second in the blue-green.

stem: Draw a neat, labelled energy level diagram for H atom showing the transitions. Explain the series of spectral lines for H atom, whose fixed inner orbit numbers are 3 and 4 respectively.
solution:
The two series of the hydrogen spectrum whose fixed inner orbit numbers are 3 and 4 are the **Paschen series** and the **Brackett series**.

**The energy level diagram.** Draw a set of horizontal lines, one for each value of the orbit number \(n\), against a vertical axis marked as the total energy \(E\) of the electron in electronvolt.

- The lowest line, labelled \(n = 1\), is drawn at \(E_1 = -13.6\text{ eV}\), and above it the lines for \(n = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, \ldots\) at \(E_n = -13.6/n^{2}\text{ eV}\), that is at \(-3.4\text{ eV}\), \(-1.51\text{ eV}\), \(-0.85\text{ eV}\), \(-0.54\text{ eV}\) and \(-0.38\text{ eV}\). The lines crowd closer together as \(n\) increases.
- The topmost line, labelled \(n = \infty\), is drawn at \(E = 0\), and the region above it is shaded and marked as the ionised atom.
- Every transition is shown as a downward vertical arrow drawn from the higher level to the lower level, because a photon is emitted when the electron falls.
- The group of arrows drawn from \(n = 4, 5, 6, \ldots\) down to the \(n = 3\) line is labelled **Paschen series**, and the group drawn from \(n = 5, 6, 7, \ldots\) down to the \(n = 4\) line is labelled **Brackett series**.

**Paschen series.** Its lines are emitted when the electron falls from an outer orbit \(m = 4, 5, 6, \ldots\) to the fixed inner orbit \(n = 3\). Their wavelengths are given by

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R_H\left(\dfrac{1}{3^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{m^{2}}\right), \qquad m = 4, 5, 6, \ldots\)

with \(R_H = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\text{ m}^{-1}\). The first line of the series \((m = 4)\) lies at \(1.876 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}\) and the series limit, reached as \(m \rightarrow \infty\), at

\(\lambda_{\min} = \dfrac{3^{2}}{R_H} = 8204\text{ \AA}\)

so the whole series lies in the infrared region.

**Brackett series.** Its lines are emitted when the electron falls from an outer orbit \(m = 5, 6, 7, \ldots\) to the fixed inner orbit \(n = 4\):

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R_H\left(\dfrac{1}{4^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{m^{2}}\right), \qquad m = 5, 6, 7, \ldots\)

Its first line \((m = 5)\) lies at \(4.051 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}\) and its series limit at

\(\lambda_{\min} = \dfrac{4^{2}}{R_H} = 14586\text{ \AA}\)

so this series too lies wholly in the infrared, at wavelengths still longer than those of the Paschen series. Both series are invisible to the eye, because the energy levels \(n = 3\) and above lie close together and the photons emitted in falling to them carry too little energy to fall in the visible range.

subtopic: Law of Radioactive Decay, Half-Life and Average Life
stem: State the law of radioactive decay. Hence derive the relation \(N = N_{0}e^{- \lambda t}\). Represent it graphically.
solution:
**Statement of the law.** The rate of disintegration of a radioactive sample at any instant is directly proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present in the sample at that instant. The rate does not depend on temperature, pressure or the chemical state in which the element is present.

**Derivation.** Let \(N\) be the number of undecayed nuclei present in the sample at time \(t\), and let \(dN\) be the change in this number in a short interval \(dt\). Since nuclei disappear, \(dN\) is negative and the rate of disintegration is \(-dN/dt\). By the law,

\(-\dfrac{dN}{dt} \propto N\)

\(\therefore -\dfrac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N\)

where the constant of proportionality \(\lambda\) is called the decay constant of the substance. Separating the variables,

\(\dfrac{dN}{N} = -\lambda\,dt\)

Integrating both sides, from \(t = 0\) when the number of undecayed nuclei is \(N_0\), to time \(t\) when it is \(N\),

\(\int_{N_0}^{N}\dfrac{dN}{N} = -\lambda\int_{0}^{t}dt\)

\(\therefore \left[\ln N\right]_{N_0}^{N} = -\lambda\left[t\right]_{0}^{t}\)

\(\therefore \ln N - \ln N_0 = -\lambda t\)

\(\therefore \ln\left(\dfrac{N}{N_0}\right) = -\lambda t\)

Taking antilogarithms of both sides,

\(\therefore N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}\)

which is the required relation.

**Graphical representation.** Plot the number of undecayed nuclei \(N\) along the vertical axis against the time \(t\) along the horizontal axis.

- The curve starts on the vertical axis at \(N = N_0\), the number present at \(t = 0\).
- It falls steeply at first and then more and more slowly, because the rate of decay is itself proportional to the number of nuclei still left; the curve is an exponential decay curve.
- It approaches the time axis asymptotically and meets it only at \(t = \infty\), so the sample is in principle never completely exhausted.
- Marking the half-life \(T_{1/2}\) on the time axis, the curve has fallen to \(N_0/2\) at \(t = T_{1/2}\), to \(N_0/4\) at \(t = 2T_{1/2}\) and to \(N_0/8\) at \(t = 3T_{1/2}\), the number being halved in every further interval of one half-life.

subtopic: Law of Radioactive Decay, Half-Life and Average Life
stem: Disintegration rate of a radio-active sample is \(10^{10}\) per hour at 20 hours from the start. It reduces to \(5 \times 10^{9}\) per hour after 30 hours. Calculate the decay constant.
solution:
The activity of a sample, that is its disintegration rate, is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present, so it decays exponentially with time:

\(A = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}\)

Let \(A_1 = 10^{10}\) per hour be the activity at \(t_1 = 20\text{ h}\) and \(A_2 = 5 \times 10^{9}\) per hour the activity at \(t_2 = 30\text{ h}\). Then

\(A_1 = A_0 e^{-\lambda t_1}\) and \(A_2 = A_0 e^{-\lambda t_2}\)

Dividing the second by the first, \(A_0\) cancels and

\(\dfrac{A_2}{A_1} = e^{-\lambda(t_2 - t_1)}\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{5 \times 10^{9}}{10^{10}} = e^{-\lambda(30 - 20)}\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{1}{2} = e^{-10\lambda}\), that is \(e^{10\lambda} = 2\)

Taking natural logarithms of both sides,

\(\therefore 10\lambda = \ln 2 = 0.693\)

\(\therefore \lambda = 0.0693\text{ h}^{-1}\)

Expressed in SI units,

\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.0693}{3600} = 1.925 \times 10^{-5}\text{ s}^{-1}\)

Check: the activity given falls to exactly half its value in the ten hours between the two readings, so the half-life of the sample is \(10\text{ h}\); and \(T_{1/2} = 0.693/\lambda = 0.693/0.0693 = 10\text{ h}\), which agrees.

subtopic: Law of Radioactive Decay, Half-Life and Average Life
stem: Derive an expression for law of radioactive decay. Define one becquerel (Bq).
solution:
**The law.** The rate of disintegration of a radioactive sample at any instant is directly proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present in the sample at that instant.

**Derivation.** Let \(N\) be the number of undecayed nuclei present at time \(t\), and let \(dN\) be the change in this number in a short interval \(dt\). Since nuclei disappear, \(dN\) is negative and the disintegration rate is \(-dN/dt\). By the law,

\(-\dfrac{dN}{dt} \propto N\)

\(\therefore -\dfrac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N\)

where \(\lambda\), the constant of proportionality, is the decay constant of the substance. Separating the variables,

\(\dfrac{dN}{N} = -\lambda\,dt\)

Integrating both sides, from \(t = 0\) when the number of undecayed nuclei is \(N_0\), to time \(t\) when it is \(N\),

\(\int_{N_0}^{N}\dfrac{dN}{N} = -\lambda\int_{0}^{t}dt\)

\(\therefore \ln N - \ln N_0 = -\lambda t\)

\(\therefore \ln\left(\dfrac{N}{N_0}\right) = -\lambda t\)

Taking antilogarithms of both sides,

\(\therefore N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}\)

which is the expression for the law of radioactive decay: the number of undecayed nuclei falls off exponentially with time.

**One becquerel.** The activity of a radioactive sample is its rate of disintegration,

\(A = -\dfrac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N\)

and its SI unit is the becquerel (Bq). **One becquerel is the activity of a radioactive sample in which one nucleus disintegrates per second**, that is \(1\text{ Bq} = 1\text{ disintegration per second}\). The older unit, the curie, is related to it by \(1\text{ Ci} = 3.7 \times 10^{10}\text{ Bq}\).

subtopic: Law of Radioactive Decay, Half-Life and Average Life
stem: The decay constant of radioactive substance is \(4.33 \times 10^{- 4}\) per year. Calculate its half life period.
solution:
The half-life \(T_{1/2}\) of a radioactive substance is the time in which the number of undecayed nuclei falls to half its initial value. Putting \(N = N_0/2\) and \(t = T_{1/2}\) in the law of radioactive decay \(N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}\),

\(\dfrac{N_0}{2} = N_0 e^{-\lambda T_{1/2}}\)

\(\therefore e^{\lambda T_{1/2}} = 2\)

Taking natural logarithms,

\(\lambda T_{1/2} = \ln 2 = 0.693\)

\(\therefore T_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda}\)

Here the decay constant is \(\lambda = 4.33 \times 10^{-4}\) per year, so

\(T_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{4.33 \times 10^{-4}}\)

\(\therefore T_{1/2} = 1600\text{ years}\)

Check: substituting the result back, \(\lambda T_{1/2} = 4.33 \times 10^{-4} \times 1600 = 0.693\), which is \(\ln 2\), as the definition of half-life requires.

stem: With the help of a neat labelled diagram, describe the Geiger-Marsden experiment. What is mass defect?
solution:
**The Geiger-Marsden experiment.** The labelled diagram of the apparatus shows the following parts.

- A **source of alpha particles**, a radioactive substance such as bismuth-214, enclosed in a thick lead block with a fine hole bored in it, so that a narrow, well collimated beam of alpha particles emerges in one direction only.
- A **thin gold foil**, only about \(10^{-7}\text{ m}\) thick, placed in the path of the beam as the target. Gold is used because it can be beaten into a foil only a few hundred atoms thick.
- A **movable detector**, a zinc sulphide screen viewed through a microscope, mounted on an arm so that it can be turned to any angle about the foil. An alpha particle striking the screen produces a tiny flash of light, a scintillation, which is counted.
- The **scattering angle \(\theta\)**, marked in the diagram as the angle between the original direction of the beam and the direction in which the detector is set.
- The whole apparatus enclosed in an **evacuated chamber**, so that the alpha particles are not scattered by collisions with air molecules.

**Observations.** Most of the alpha particles passed straight through the foil undeviated, or were deflected through very small angles. A small fraction were deflected through large angles, and about one in eight thousand was turned back through an angle greater than \(90^{\circ}\).

**Conclusions.** Since the great majority of the alpha particles pass through undeviated, most of the space inside an atom is empty. Since a few are turned through large angles and some are turned right back, the whole of the positive charge and almost the whole of the mass of the atom must be concentrated in an extremely small region at its centre, called the nucleus, whose intense repulsive electrostatic field is able to turn a fast alpha particle back. From the fraction turned back, the radius of the nucleus is of the order of \(10^{-14}\text{ m}\), about ten thousand times smaller than the atom itself. The electrons revolve round this nucleus, and it is this picture that is called Rutherford's nuclear model of the atom.

**Mass defect.** The mass of a nucleus is always found to be less than the sum of the masses of the protons and the neutrons of which it is made. This difference of mass is called the mass defect of the nucleus:

\(\Delta m = \left[Zm_p + (A - Z)m_n\right] - M\)

where \(Z\) is the atomic number, \(A\) the mass number, \(m_p\) and \(m_n\) the masses of a free proton and a free neutron and \(M\) the mass of the nucleus. So defined, \(\Delta m\) is positive for every stable nucleus, since energy has to be supplied to pull the nucleus apart into its separate nucleons.

The missing mass appears as the energy given out when the free nucleons come together to form the nucleus, and by Einstein's mass-energy relation the binding energy of the nucleus is

\(E_B = \Delta m\,c^{2}\)

If \(\Delta m\) is expressed in unified atomic mass units \((\text{u})\), then, since \(1\text{ u}\) is equivalent to \(931.5\text{ MeV}\),

\(E_B = \Delta m \times 931.5\text{ MeV}\)
